raw.quick_summary: The exercise shows that identical printed labels do not make events identical: the assembly “Ready” event is {p,q}, while the inspection “Ready” event is {q,r}. Their intersection is {q}, their union is {p,q,r}, and the corresponding probabilities are 1/2, 1/4, and 3/4.

key_concepts.explanation: The possible outcomes are the four equally likely tickets {p,q,r,s}.
In the assembly department, Ready refers to the event {p,q}.
In the inspection department, Ready refers to the event {q,r}.
The two events remain different because they belong to different departments and have different ticket membership, even though both are printed as “Ready.”
The two Ready events intersect at the shared ticket q, so their intersection is {q}.
Together, the two Ready events contain p, q, and r, so their union is {p,q,r}.
Because the four tickets are equally likely, the two Ready events each have probability 1/2, their intersection has probability 1/4, and their union has probability 3/4.

concept_map.reason: The main learning challenge is distinguishing two same-labeled events and relating their memberships to intersection, union, and probability.

comparison.reason: Comparison is useful as a supporting activity, but the dominant structure is the connected relationship among the sample space, two events, and their set operations.

learning_path.title: Separating Same-Labeled Events with Sets and Probabilities
learning_path.reason: The exercise supports a short progression from outcomes, to event membership, to identity, set operations, and probability calculations.

steps.title: Start with the equally likely tickets
steps.learning_goal: Identify the finite sample space and the probability of each ticket.
steps.explanation: The sample space is {p,q,r,s}. Since the four tickets are equally likely, each individual ticket has probability 1/4.
steps.connection_to_previous: This establishes the outcomes from which both department events are formed.

steps.title: Record each department’s event membership
steps.learning_goal: Represent each Ready event as a set of tickets.
steps.explanation: Assembly Ready is {p,q}; inspection Ready is {q,r}. Set membership preserves which tickets each department includes.
steps.connection_to_previous: The events are subsets of the sample space identified in the previous step.

steps.title: Keep the event identities separate
steps.learning_goal: Understand why the same printed word does not denote one merged event.
steps.explanation: The two events have different department contexts and different memberships. The shared label “Ready” is not enough to identify them as the same event.
steps.connection_to_previous: Comparing the two membership sets reveals why their identities must remain distinct.

steps.title: Find the intersection and union
steps.learning_goal: Use membership comparison to compute the shared and combined outcomes.
steps.explanation: The only ticket in both sets is q, so the intersection is {q}. Combining all tickets appearing in either set gives the union {p,q,r}.
steps.connection_to_previous: Once the two events are kept separate, their shared and total membership can be compared directly.

steps.title: Convert set sizes into probabilities
steps.learning_goal: Calculate event, intersection, and union probabilities in the equally likely space.
steps.explanation: With four equally likely tickets, |{p,q}|/4 = 1/2, |{q,r}|/4 = 1/2, |{q}|/4 = 1/4, and |{p,q,r}|/4 = 3/4.
steps.connection_to_previous: The probabilities follow from counting the members of the sets found in the previous step.

checkpoint_questions.question: Why are the two events different even though both are labeled “Ready”?

options.text: They belong to different departments and contain different ticket sets.
The word Ready has two different probabilities.
They are different only because q appears in both.
They cannot be compared because they use the same label.

checkpoint_questions.explanation: Event identity depends on the department/context and membership set, not merely on the printed label.

checkpoint_questions.question: Which ticket belongs to both the assembly Ready event and the inspection Ready event?
checkpoint_questions.explanation: Assembly Ready is {p,q} and inspection Ready is {q,r}; their only shared ticket is q.

checkpoint_questions.question: What is the probability of the union of the two Ready events?
checkpoint_questions.explanation: The union is {p,q,r}, which contains three of the four equally likely tickets, so its probability is 3/4.
